items.title: AI co-scientists are revolutionizing how research is done
items.author: Elie Dolgin
items.blurb: Elie Dolgin surveys the AI ‘co-scientist’ systems now generating hypotheses, designing experiments and analysing data in labs — and finds that humans are still the ones who have to decide what makes sense.

items.title: Did OpenAI solve the wrong Navier-Stokes problem?
items.blurb: OpenAI’s Navier–Stokes proof appears eligible for the $1-million Millennium Prize — but, Scientific American reports, only by way of a controversial loophole in how the problem is posed.

items.title: What’s Really Behind the Baby Bust?
items.author: Margaret Talbot
items.blurb: Reviewing Anna Louise Sussman’s ‘Inconceivable’, Margaret Talbot asks why people say they want more children than they have — whether modern life is stopping them, or our ideas about a good life have changed.

items.title: China punishes prominent academics exposed by research sleuth
items.author: Xiaoying You
items.blurb: Several prominent Chinese scientists investigated for research-integrity violations by the video-blogger ‘Student Geng’ have now faced disciplinary measures, Xiaoying You reports — a rare case of a public sleuth forcing institutional action.

items.title: What a Trump order to put political appointees in charge of NIH funding would mean for science
items.blurb: Advocates and scientists warn that a reported executive order giving political appointees power over NIH research grants would ‘upend’ U.S. science and its peer-review system.

items.title: Members of Congress push back on plan to create a commission of political appointees to review NIH grants
items.author: Anil Oza and Chelsea Cirruzzo
items.blurb: OMB director Russell Vought is pushing an executive order that would create a commission — including himself and NIH director Jay Bhattacharya, with unanimous sign-off required — to review every NIH grant; several members of Congress have voiced strong opposition.

items.title: Further results on AI and labor market reallocation
items.author: Tyler Cowen
items.blurb: Cowen flags a new paper that combines CPS and JOLTS data with OpenAI and Lightcast measures of AI exposure and adoption to document how AI has changed stocks and flows in the US labour market.

items.title: Mathematicians use AI to find mysterious symmetries, solving decades-old problem
items.blurb: Six mathematicians used AI to spot symmetries and approximate polynomials, finding a degree-23 polynomial that settles the inverse Galois problem for the sporadic group M₂₃ — while a parallel crowdsourced race found all 25,000 cases for 24 roots, with humans using minimal AI winning.

items.title: Why mathematicians are hiding research results in zero-knowledge proofs
items.blurb: Google used a zero-knowledge proof to show quantum computers could break encryption by decade’s end without revealing the algorithm; outside experts reproduced and improved the result within weeks, a test case for whether secrecy can survive in mathematics.

items.title: Hundreds of ‘free’ academic journals have started charging fees
items.author: Dalmeet Singh Chawla
items.blurb: A study tracking diamond open-access journals finds a growing number of ‘free’ titles switching to fee-charging models — especially over the past few years — Dalmeet Singh Chawla reports.

items.title: The economics of late grandmotherhood
items.author: Tyler Cowen
items.blurb: A new paper shows how fertility delays compound across generations: under the 1960 first-birth schedule median grandmotherhood came at 44; under the 2024 schedule it is 57, cutting into the healthy years grandmothers have with grandchildren.

items.author: Chris Simms

items.title: Why I send my kid to low-income urban public schools
items.author: Matthew Yglesias

items.title: How the Absence of Shame Weakens Democracy
items.author: Jay Caspian Kang

items.title: RFK, Jr., is focusing attention on electromagnetic fields. Here’s what the science says about exposure
America’s Allies Are No Longer Waiting for Trump to Leave
items.author: Vivian Salama

items.title: How to stay smart in the age of AI: the science of critical thinking
items.author: Helen Pearson
items.blurb: Helen Pearson reviews the early literature on whether AI blunts memory and reasoning — Nature’s feature opens with an education researcher realizing students could outsource his entire course to AI — and what the science says about keeping the brain sharp.

items.title: Where Is the U.S. Beating China on A.I., and Where Is It Lagging?
items.author: Dustin Volz and Cade Metz
items.blurb: As Xi Jinping visits Washington, Dustin Volz and Cade Metz map where China lags the United States on AI development in key areas — and where Beijing holds the advantages.

items.title: The Price of Intelligence is Falling Rapidly
items.author: Alex Tabarrok
items.blurb: Alex Tabarrok flags an Epoch AI report by Emberson and Roodman: over the past three years the cost of a given level of AI performance has fallen about 47% per quarter — a 13-fold drop every year.

items.title: In praise of human teachers: universities must resist outsourcing everything to AI
items.blurb: Nature’s editorial argues that with universities preparing for an AI revolution in teaching and assessment, and teachers already reporting chatbots crowding out reasoning, human teachers who convey the excitement of thinking are irreplaceable.

items.title: China Has No Use for AI Doomerism
items.author: Liza Lin
items.blurb: Liza Lin reports that China’s most prominent AI companies have no use for doomerism — they are focused on beating the U.S., no matter the cost.

items.title: Europe Can’t Get Out of Its Own Way
items.author: Andrew McAfee
items.blurb: Andrew McAfee argues EU productivity has slid from 95% of U.S. levels to 20% below, and that even full implementation of the Draghi report would not fix it: the problem is not too little support for competitiveness but layers of labour, tax and tech regulation that block a U.S.-style startup ecosystem.

items.title: What China’s Vibe-Coding Capital Can Tell Us About the A.I. Boom
items.author: Afra Wang
items.blurb: Afra Wang visits Liangzhu, a small town outside Hangzhou where tech workers have flocked to escape China’s corporate culture and build their future with AI.

items.title: Claude discovers a novel enzyme system with CRISPR-like repeats
items.blurb: Anthropic’s new life-sciences group set ~950 Claude agents loose on 200,000 reverse transcriptases for 21 hours; they surfaced a previously uncharacterized phage enzyme system with CRISPR-like repeat arrays, though its biological function remains unknown and the result is an Anthropic-authored preprint.

items.author: Michael Schuman

items.title: Agent of whom?
Best clock ever: timekeeper based on lutetium atoms wows researchers
items.author: Elizabeth Gibney

items.title: Biology Might Not Be Quantum, but Its Math Is Quantumlike
items.author: Elise Cutts

items.title: Lack of female researchers and participants in regenerative-medicine research holds everyone back
items.author: Doris A. Taylor

items.title: AI solves 79-year-old math mystery of six-dimensional spheres
items.blurb: Manon Bischoff and Joseph Howlett report that Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge used Claude to settle the 1947 Hopf problem — whether a six-dimensional sphere admits a complex structure — with a 100-plus-page proof that other researchers reconstructed and formalized within days.

items.title: AI system helps lab devices ‘talk’ with each other — streamlining research
items.author: Kaia Glickman
items.blurb: Kaia Glickman reports on the Model Hardware Standard, a framework from Anthropic and HHMI’s Janelia campus that lets instruments from different vendors talk to one another and lets an AI agent control them and orchestrate experiments — attacking the notoriously hard job of wiring a lab together.

items.title: China’s open AI models are testing America’s approach to AI safety
items.blurb: Peter Hall argues that freely downloadable Chinese open-weight models undercut the developer-controlled safeguards American labs rely on — when OpenAI’s model breached Hugging Face, investigators used a Chinese open model to analyse the attack because U.S. systems refused — complicating the AI-safety talks on the Trump–Xi agenda.

items.title: There Is No A.I. “Race”
items.author: Chang Che
items.blurb: Chang Che draws on Nathan Rosenberg and Jeffrey Ding’s diffusion theory — Britain invented the steam turbine but America electrified — to argue that being first in AI is a poor predictor of who wins, and that the ‘race’ framing crowds out the case for pacing the frontier.

items.title: Peter Thiel on AI and tech stagnation and democracy
items.author: Tyler Cowen
items.blurb: Tyler Cowen flags what he calls ‘one of the very best Peter Thiel outputs’ — fresh material on AI, technological stagnation and democracy.
